What I did

I updated Jaime’s existing regressions to use the group’s November 2 decisions. Each AI model has one regression. A question can have several features at once. The model estimates an expected preference score: win = 1, loss = 0, and tie or both bad = 0.5. With half points, this score is not simply the probability of winning a decisive vote.

The descriptive fit below uses 106,602 votes from April through July, represented by two model-side rows per vote. There are 48 fitted models. As in Jaime’s original code, flagged review cases are excluded from the fit. The original data are unchanged.

Response and predictors

The response is the model’s score for that vote. These are the only predictors; all describe the question, before the AI writes an answer.

Feature Meaning
is_code The question involves programming.
math The question involves mathematics.
creative_writing The question asks for creative writing.
instruction_following The question contains specific instructions.
complexity The question is complex.
creativity The task needs creative thinking.
domain_knowledge The task needs subject knowledge.
problem_solving The task needs problem-solving steps.
real_world The task has a practical, real-world use.
specificity The task is specific and well defined.
technical_accuracy The task needs technical accuracy.

Response length, formatting, price and tokens are not predictors. The opponent is not a predictor in these separate regressions (group decision 5).

This is the actual regression specification:

glm(y ~ is_code + math + creative_writing + instruction_following +
      complexity + creativity + domain_knowledge + problem_solving +
      real_world + specificity + technical_accuracy,
    family = quasibinomial(), data = votes_for_one_model)

The default uses lambda = 0, so these are ordinary glm() fits. The updated function also accepts ridge: ajustar_modelos(datos, lambda = ...). It shrinks only the 11 feature effects, never the intercept. Mark will choose lambda using train only; this report does not choose it by looking at July.

The regressions: full R output

A positive math coefficient means a higher fitted preference score on math questions, holding the other features fixed. It is a change in log-odds, not a percentage-point change or a causal effect. For example, Gemini’s math coefficient is 0.085. P-values below are nominal: the rows are not independent across models.

Open each example to see its complete summary() output, including coefficients, dispersion and convergence information. The third example has the fewest votes in this descriptive fit.

Feature effects for all 48 models

Blue means a higher preference score when a feature is present; red means a lower score. These are log-odds coefficients, with the other features held fixed. The intercept is omitted from this chart. Full values, including all intercepts, are in R/resultados/coeficientes_por_modelo.csv.

Descriptive fit: all April–July votes, half points, no ridge.

Does it predict unseen votes?

The descriptive fit above uses all months and is not a test result. The table below comes directly from Mark’s saved evaluation. Mark fits on April–June only and evaluates decisive July votes where both models were seen in train. Ties and both bad affect the half-point training fit but are not scored as winners in the test.

Method July votes Correct Accuracy (%) Log-loss (lower is better)
General Bradley–Terry ranking (decisive train votes) 20416 13164 64.5 0.6340
General win rate (half points in train) 20416 13171 64.5 0.6378
Separate regressions (half points in train) 20416 13298 65.1 0.6321

The separate regressions gain 0.66 percentage points in accuracy over the general Bradley–Terry ranking: a small improvement. Their log-loss is clearly better than the general win rate. Against Bradley–Terry, the log-loss difference is small and Mark’s interval reaches zero; we cannot claim a clear improvement in probability quality. These statements follow the correction in docs/12-decisiones-2-11.md.

Top 3 by task

top3() averages fitted scores over real questions with each feature, allowing the other features to vary. Here the descriptive fit uses all months. Only models with at least 100 votes in July can be recommended. Versions remain separate. These are task recommendations, not a new test evaluation.

An optional budget filters output price per million tokens, not total cost per answer. Unknown prices are excluded only when a budget is supplied. For example:

top3("math", ajustes, precio_max = 2)

Limits and next step

  • Each vote contributes two model-side rows; the separate fits are dependent.
  • The main test is one time split, April–June versus July.
  • Four models appear only in July and cannot be tested with that training set.

The combined Bradley–Terry model is a separate next task. It will use one row per vote and account directly for the opponent. This report does not include it.

Prepared by Nessim Betesh with assistance from ChatGPT/Codex. Existing model code by Jaime and held-out evaluation by Mark. AI-generated code and text were checked against the repository’s data, saved outputs and rules.
